title: Stream Processing
subtitle: Apache Flink · Spark Structured Streaming · Kafka Streams · Google Dataflow (Beam)
lego: Robots standing beside the conveyor belt that sort, count and combine pieces as they fly past, instead of waiting for the belt to stop.
summary: Stream processing runs continuous computations over unbounded event streams: filters, enrichments, joins, and windowed aggregations (tumbling, sliding, session). Event time vs processing time matters. Watermarks estimate when a window has seen all its data, and allowed lateness plus triggers decide what to do with stragglers. State (counts, joins) lives in local stores such as RocksDB, and periodic distributed snapshots (Flink checkpoints) give exactly-once state on failure.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Real-time features (clicks in the last 5 minutes), fraud detection, live dashboards, inventory and price propagation, alerting.
Continuously materializing views into a cache, a search index or an OLAP store.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Harder to test and operate than batch. State migrations and reprocessing need planning.
Exactly-once holds end to end only with transactional or idempotent sinks.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Backpressure from a slow sink stalls the whole job and consumer lag grows.
State grows without bound from joins with no TTL, and checkpoints get slower and slower.
A skewed key (one mega-merchant) pins one task while the others idle.

title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
subtitle: Debezium · Datastream · Netflix DBLog · Kafka Connect
lego: A camera pointed at the database's diary, copying every line to the conveyor belt the moment it's written.
summary: CDC tails the database's replication log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) and emits every insert, update and delete as an ordered event, usually into Kafka. Downstream systems (search index, cache invalidation, data lake, feature store) stay in sync without dual writes from the application. An initial snapshot plus the ongoing log gives a complete copy.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Feeding the lakehouse and BigQuery in near-real time, invalidating caches, updating search indexes, publishing outbox events.

sections.title: Watch out
items: Schema changes flow downstream. Use a schema registry with compatibility rules.
Replication slots that aren't consumed make the source database retain WAL until its disk fills.

links.title: DBLog: A Watermark Based Change-Data-Capture Framework

title: Lambda vs Kappa Architecture
subtitle: Batch plus speed layer, or one streaming path with replay
lego: Build the model twice (a careful overnight version plus a quick live sketch), or build it once on the conveyor belt and simply rewind the belt when you need to rebuild.
summary: The Lambda architecture runs a batch layer (accurate, recomputed daily) and a speed layer (approximate, real time), and merges them at query time. The cost is two codebases that drift apart. The Kappa architecture uses a single stream-processing path over a replayable log (Kafka with long retention, or a lakehouse table), and reprocesses by replaying into a new version of the job. Modern stacks often blend the two: streaming for freshness, and a lakehouse where batch and streaming read and write the same tables.

sections.title: Choose
items: Lambda when batch logic is heavy (large ML training features) and a streaming approximation is acceptable.
Kappa when one codebase and one source of truth matter more, and replay is affordable.

links.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know

title: Apache Spark
subtitle: Spark SQL / DataFrames · Dataproc · Databricks · EMR
lego: A crew of a hundred builders who each take a pile of pieces, sort them in parallel, swap pieces with each other when needed, and hand back one finished model.
summary: A distributed compute engine. A driver turns your DataFrame or SQL code into a DAG of stages. Narrow transformations (map, filter) run in parallel per partition; wide ones (groupBy, join) shuffle data across the network between stages. The Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine generate efficient plans, and Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) re-plans at runtime: it coalesces partitions, switches join strategies and splits skewed partitions. Spark reads and writes Parquet, ORC, Iceberg and Delta tables on GCS, S3 or HDFS, and also runs Structured Streaming and MLlib.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Batch ETL and ELT over GBs to PBs, feature engineering for training, large joins and aggregations, backfills.
Batch scoring, or preparing data for Ray and GPU training jobs.

sections.title: Performance levers
items: Avoid shuffles. Broadcast small tables in joins, and filter and project early (predicate pushdown into Parquet).
Right-size partitions (about 128–256 MB each). Fix skew with AQE skew joins or by salting hot keys.
Cache only what is reused. Use columnar formats and partition tables by date.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Executor OOM from skew or huge shuffles. Driver OOM from collect() on big data.
The small-files problem: thousands of tiny outputs slow every downstream job. Compact them.
Spot or preemptible executor loss causes recomputation. Enable graceful decommissioning and checkpoints for long lineages.

title: Workflow Orchestration
subtitle: Apache Airflow · Cloud Composer · Dagster · Argo Workflows
lego: The foreman's schedule board: which crew builds which section, in what order, at what time, and what to redo when a section collapses.
summary: An orchestrator defines pipelines as DAGs of tasks with dependencies, schedules them (cron, data-aware or event triggers), retries failures, backfills historical intervals, and records run state and lineage. Airflow (Cloud Composer on GCP) is the de facto standard. Dagster is asset-centric, and Argo runs Kubernetes-native steps. Tasks should call out to engines (Spark, BigQuery, Ray); the orchestrator coordinates, it doesn't compute.

sections.title: Best practices
items: Make every task idempotent and parameterized by the logical date: overwrite the partition for that date, never append blindly.
Keep DAG files lightweight (no heavy imports or queries at parse time). Pass pointers such as GCS paths between tasks, not data.
Use sensors or deferrable operators for upstream data, set SLAs and alerting, and cap concurrency so backfills don't overload the warehouse.

title: Lakehouse Table Formats
subtitle: Apache Iceberg · Delta Lake · Apache Hudi · BigLake
lego: Adds an inventory ledger to the giant storage bins, so everyone agrees exactly which pieces make up version 42 of the model, even while others add pieces.
summary: Open table formats put a transactional metadata layer (snapshots, manifests, a transaction log) over Parquet files in object storage. They provide ACID commits with concurrent writers, schema evolution, hidden partitioning, time travel ('as of' queries), row-level upserts and deletes (MERGE), and compaction. Spark, Flink, Trino and BigQuery can all share the same tables. That brings warehouse reliability to cheap lake storage.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Bronze/silver/gold (raw → cleaned → aggregated) zones on GCS or S3. Streaming upserts from CDC. Reproducible training sets through time travel.

sections.title: Maintenance
items: Compact small files, expire old snapshots, and clean up orphan files on a schedule. Otherwise metadata and storage costs balloon.

links.title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores (VLDB 2020)

title: Columnar Formats & Warehouses
subtitle: Parquet · ORC · BigQuery · Snowflake · Apache Pinot / Druid
lego: Store all the red pieces together, all the blue pieces together, and so on, so a question about only red pieces never has to open the other drawers.
summary: Columnar storage keeps each column contiguous and compressed (dictionary, run-length and bit-packing encodings), with min/max statistics per row group. Queries read only the columns they need and skip blocks that can't match. Warehouses such as BigQuery (built on Dremel) separate storage from compute and run massively parallel SQL. Real-time OLAP engines (Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse) serve sub-second analytics on fresh streaming data.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Partition by date and cluster or sort by common filter columns. Avoid SELECT * on wide tables because you pay per byte scanned.
Use a warehouse for analysts and BI. Use OLAP engines for user-facing, high-QPS dashboards.

links.title: Dremel: A Decade of Interactive SQL Analysis at Web Scale (VLDB 2020)

title: Batch Pipeline Design Principles
subtitle: Idempotency · backfills · late data · data quality · lineage
lego: Instructions written so that any step can be redone from scratch on any day and produce exactly the same section of the model.
summary: Reliable batch pipelines follow a few rules. Treat each run as a pure function of its input partitions: an idempotent overwrite of the output partition for the logical date. Keep raw data immutable so you can recompute anything. Make backfills a first-class operation. Handle late-arriving data by reprocessing a trailing window. Put data-quality checks (row counts, null rates, schema, freshness, distribution drift) as gates between stages. Record lineage so you know what to rerun when an upstream table is fixed.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Write to a staging location, validate, then atomically swap or commit (table-format commit or partition overwrite).
Use data contracts and a schema registry between producing and consuming teams.
Set freshness SLAs per table, with alerts before consumers notice.
Size for the backfill case: 90 days at once, with capped concurrency.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Append-only reruns double-count. Silent schema changes produce null columns. A job that 'succeeds' on empty input overwrites good data with nothing.

title: Daily Batch ETL to the Lakehouse
subtitle: GCS + Spark + Iceberg + Airflow + BigQuery
lego: Every night the crew unloads the day's delivery trucks, sorts the pieces into labelled bins, checks nothing is broken, and updates the showroom by morning.
summary: Every night, ingest the previous day's orders, clickstream and inventory snapshots (about 5 TB) from operational systems. Clean, join and aggregate them into analytics tables and ML training features, available by 6 AM with guaranteed correctness and the ability to backfill any day.
steps: Land raw data in a GCS bronze bucket partitioned by dt=YYYY-MM-DD: database exports or CDC from Kafka via Kafka Connect, plus event files. Raw data is immutable.
An Airflow (Cloud Composer) DAG runs per logical date, with sensors waiting for each upstream partition.
Spark jobs on Dataproc clean and deduplicate into silver Iceberg tables, using MERGE on business keys so reruns are idempotent.
Data-quality gates (row counts against the prior 7 days, null rates, schema, freshness) must pass. On failure, stop and alert rather than publish.
Gold aggregates and features are written as a partition overwrite for that date, then exposed to BigQuery as BigLake or external tables.
Publish a 'dataset ready' event (Pub/Sub or Kafka) that triggers downstream training and feature materialization. Lineage is recorded.

sections.title: Numbers
items: 5 TB a day of raw input over a 4-hour window needs about 350 MB/s sustained, which is roughly 50–100 executors depending on the transforms.

sections.title: Break it
items: An upstream table arrives 3 hours late: sensors wait, the freshness SLA alert fires, and the pipeline catches up without manual reruns.
A bug is found in the silver logic from last month: backfill 30 dates with capped concurrency. Every task overwrites its partition, so nothing is double-counted.

title: Real-Time Clickstream Analytics
subtitle: Kafka → Flink → OLAP + lakehouse
lego: Count every visitor's footsteps as they walk through the store, and put the live tally on a big board at the entrance.
summary: Show merchants live dashboards (views, add-to-carts and conversion per product in the last 1–60 minutes) over 500,000 events per second, while keeping the full history for batch analytics and ML.
steps: Web and app SDKs send events to a collector behind the edge and gateway, which validates the schema and produces to Kafka keyed by session or product.
A Flink job deduplicates by event ID, enriches from a cached product dimension, and computes event-time windowed aggregates with watermarks.
Aggregates are upserted into a real-time OLAP store (Pinot or Druid) that serves dashboard queries in under a second.
Raw events also stream into an Iceberg table on GCS (the lake sink) for nightly batch jobs and ML features.
Late events inside the allowed lateness update the windows. Later ones are fixed by the nightly batch recompute.

sections.title: Break it
items: Kill a Flink TaskManager: the job restores from its checkpoint and reprocesses from committed Kafka offsets, with no double counts because the sink upserts.
A viral product creates a hot key: pre-aggregate locally before the keyed shuffle.

title: Drill: Bad Data & the Big Backfill
subtitle: Break your batch pipeline on purpose
lego: Sneak a box of wrong-coloured pieces into the delivery and see whether the night crew notices before the showroom opens.
summary: In your batch pipeline, inject three faults: an empty upstream file, a column renamed upstream, and duplicated input records. Then run a 60-day backfill. Does bad data reach the gold tables and dashboards, and does the backfill overload anything?
steps: Hypothesis: quality gates block all three faults, and the backfill finishes under the concurrency cap without hurting production jobs.
Inject the empty file. The row-count check against the trailing average must fail the run before the overwrite.
Inject the schema rename. Schema validation or the data contract must fail loudly, not produce null columns.
Inject duplicates. MERGE or deduplication on business keys must keep the gold counts unchanged.
Run the 60-day backfill with max_active_runs capped, and watch warehouse slots, the Spark cluster and the freshness of today's run.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Batch failures are usually silent. A pipeline that errors is better than one that publishes wrong numbers.
